title: Giving Claude a Second Opinion: Bridging a Sandboxed Agent to a Model It Can't Reach
summary: A file-queue bridge between Claude and GLM, and the two rounds of adversarial review that made it more reliable.
content:
My university (UIUC) runs an LLM gateway called Lumen that gives students free
API access to a rotating set of models. GLM-5.3-Flash landed there recently —
a fast multimodal model from Zhipu AI, MIT-licensed, trained on domestic
Chinese silicon.

I use Claude as my daily driver. A colleague mentioned he'd been feeding
Claude's plans to GLM for adversarial review, and that the pair worked well
together. That is a genuinely good idea: two model families trained by
different labs on different data have different blind spots. The one thing an
LLM is worst at is auditing its own reasoning.

So I wanted Claude to be able to consult GLM *on its own* — not me shuttling
text between two tabs.

That turned out to be blocked by something I didn't expect, and the workaround
is the interesting part of this post.

---

## TL;DR — the setup

**What you get:** Claude, running in its sandbox, can send a prompt to any HTTP
API on your machine's network — including ones its own egress proxy blocks —
and read the answer back, with no copy-pasting from you.

**How:** a file-queue daemon on your machine. Claude writes a job file into a
folder it shares with you; a small Python process on your side polls that
folder, makes the actual API call, and writes the answer back.

```
Claude (sandboxed)              your machine (real network)
        │                                  │
        ├── writes in/<id>.json ──────────▶│
        │                                  ├─ watcher.py polls
        │                                  ├─ calls the API  ✓
        │◀───────── out/<id>.json ─────────┤
```

**Prerequisites:** Python 3.8+, an API key, and a folder your agent can read
and write.

### Option A: hand this to your Claude

Paste the block below into Claude (Cowork, Claude Code, or anything with file
access to your machine). It contains everything needed.

````text
I want to set up a file-queue bridge so you can call an HTTP API that your own
sandbox network cannot reach, by relaying the request through my machine.

Context:
- My API endpoint: <PASTE ENDPOINT, e.g. https://lumen.ncsa.illinois.edu/v1/chat/completions>
- My model name:   <PASTE MODEL, e.g. glm-5.3-flash>
- My OS:           <Windows / macOS / Linux>

Please do this step by step:

1. First, TEST whether you can reach my endpoint directly from your own
   environment. Run a curl or equivalent and show me the actual result. If you
   CAN reach it, stop — we don't need this bridge at all.

2. If you cannot, test whether you can reach it from a shell on my machine
   (if you have one). Report what you find. Do not assume — run the command.

3. Ask me to connect/grant access to a working folder if you don't have one.

4. In that folder, create a `glm_bridge/` directory containing:
   - `watcher.py`  : polls in/ for *.json jobs, calls the API, writes out/*.json
   - `ask.py`      : producer helper that writes a job ATOMICALLY (tmp + rename)
                     and waits for the answer
   - `.env`        : holds my API key, mode 600
   - an autostart installer appropriate for my OS
     (Windows: Startup-folder shortcut via pythonw;
      macOS: launchd user agent; Linux: systemd --user unit)

   The watcher MUST handle these, because I have seen each one bite:
   - Never delete a job on a transient API failure. Retry with backoff, then
     move it to failed/ — never silently destroy it.
   - Treat only a SUCCESS as final. A stale failure result must not permanently
     poison that job id; resubmitting the same id has to work.
   - A job file may be read mid-write. Do not declare it malformed on the first
     parse error; wait until the file stops changing.
   - Single-instance guard, so the autostart copy and a manual launch don't
     both process the same queue.
   - Read the HTTP error body, not just the status line.
   - Back off on repeated loop errors instead of writing a traceback every second.
   - Load the key from the .env file, since launchd and systemd do not inherit
     my shell rc.

5. Install the autostart entry, start it, and show me the log.

6. Run a live end-to-end test and show me the actual response.

7. From then on: whenever your confidence in an answer is mid or low, send your
   draft through the bridge for a second opinion and show me both answers side
   by side, plus which of its criticisms you accept or reject and why.

Important: verify each step by running it. Tell me plainly if something fails
rather than assuming it worked.
````

### Option B: manual install

```bash
mkdir -p glm_bridge/{in,out,failed}
cd glm_bridge
# save watcher.py and ask.py from the "Scripts" section below
printf 'LUMEN_API_KEY=sk_your_key_here\n' > .env
chmod 600 .env
python3 watcher.py          # leave running, or install autostart below
```

Test it:

```bash
echo "Reply with exactly: BRIDGE OK" | python3 ask.py
```

---

## Why a file bridge, of all things

My first instinct was the obvious one: just have Claude `curl` the endpoint.

```
$ curl -s https://lumen.ncsa.illinois.edu/v1/chat/completions ...
exit code 56
[agent-proxy] connect_rejected — the egress proxy denied the CONNECT
```

Claude's cloud sandbox routes all outbound traffic through an allowlist proxy.
A university endpoint nobody has allowlisted is simply not reachable. Fine —
Claude also had a shell on my own machine. Surely that one works?

```
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" https://lumen.ncsa.illinois.edu/v1/models
HTTP 000
$ getent hosts lumen.ncsa.illinois.edu
(no DNS)
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" https://pypi.org
HTTP 200
```

It does not. That "shell on my machine" is itself an isolated Linux VM behind
the same allowlist proxy. DNS for the university host doesn't even resolve,
while pypi.org sails through — proving it's policy, not connectivity.

This is worth dwelling on, because it generalizes. **An agent's file access and
an agent's network access are two separate permissions, and they don't have to
agree.** Claude could read and write a folder on my machine while being unable
to make a single HTTP request to a host on my network.

And that asymmetry is exactly the opening. The folder is shared. My *real*
Python — the one outside all of this, where `pip` and my shell live — has
ordinary internet access. So the bridge is:

- Claude writes a request into the shared folder.
- A process running as *me*, with *my* network, picks it up and makes the call.
- The answer goes back into the shared folder.

No ports, no tunnels, no daemon exposed to the network. The filesystem is the
entire protocol. It works with any agent that can write a file, and any API
your machine can reach.

---

## The scripts

Final layout:

```
glm_bridge/
├── watcher.py              # the daemon
├── ask.py                  # producer helper (atomic writes)
├── .env                    # API key, mode 600
├── install_autostart.sh    # macOS / Linux
├── install_autostart.bat   # Windows
├── in/                     # jobs waiting
├── out/                    # answers
├── failed/                 # jobs that exhausted retries
└── watcher.log
```

### `watcher.py`

```python
"""
GLM Bridge Watcher v3
=====================
A tiny file-queue daemon that lets a sandboxed agent (Claude) reach an API
endpoint its own network cannot resolve, by relaying through this machine.

  in/<id>.json   ->  {"prompt": "...", "system": "..."}   (written atomically)
  out/<id>.json  <-  {"id": ..., "ok": true, "answer": "..."}
  failed/        <-  jobs that exhausted their retry budget (never silently lost)
"""
import os, json, time, glob, socket, datetime, traceback
from urllib import request, error

HERE     = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
ENV_FILE = os.path.join(HERE, ".env")

def load_env_file():
    """launchd (macOS) and systemd (Linux) do not inherit your shell rc, and a
    Windows Startup entry only sees the registry copy. A .env beside this file
    is the one mechanism that works identically everywhere."""
    try:
        with open(ENV_FILE, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
                    continue
                k, v = line.split("=", 1)
                os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip('"').strip("'"))
    except OSError:
        pass

load_env_file()

IN_DIR   = os.path.join(HERE, "in")
OUT_DIR  = os.path.join(HERE, "out")
FAIL_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, "failed")
LOG      = os.path.join(HERE, "watcher.log")

MODEL    = os.environ.get("GLM_MODEL", "glm-5.3-flash")
ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("LUMEN_ENDPOINT",
                          "https://lumen.ncsa.illinois.edu/v1/chat/completions")
try:
    TIMEOUT = int(os.environ.get("GLM_TIMEOUT", "120"))
except ValueError:
    TIMEOUT = 120                      # a bad env var must not kill us silently

MAX_ATTEMPTS  = 5
GRACE_SECONDS = 180      # after startup, network errors don't burn the budget
STUCK_SECONDS = 120      # unreadable/unparseable that long -> quarantine
LOCK_PORT     = 47301    # single-instance guard; OS frees it on death
LOG_MAX       = 5 * 1024 * 1024

STARTED_AT = time.time()
FIRST_SEEN = {}          # path -> first time we failed to read/parse it

DEFAULT_SYSTEM = (
    "You are an adversarial reviewer giving a second opinion on another AI's answer. "
    "Be direct and concise. Flag flawed assumptions, missing edge cases, and anything "
    "overlooked. If you agree, say so briefly and explain why. Do not pad."
)

# ---------- logging ----------------------------------------------------------

def log(msg):
    line = f"[{datetime.datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}] {msg}"
    try:
        if os.path.exists(LOG) and os.path.getsize(LOG) > LOG_MAX:
            os.replace(LOG, LOG + ".1")           # single-generation rotation
        with open(LOG, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(line + "\n")
    except Exception:
        pass

# ---------- single instance --------------------------------------------------

def acquire_lock():
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    try:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", LOCK_PORT))
        s.listen(1)
        return s                                  # held for process lifetime
    except OSError:
        return None

# ---------- API --------------------------------------------------------------

def ask_glm(prompt, system=None):
    key = os.environ.get("LUMEN_API_KEY", "").strip()
    if not key:
        raise RuntimeError("LUMEN_API_KEY not set in this process's environment")

    body = json.dumps({
        "model": MODEL,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": system or DEFAULT_SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user",   "content": prompt},
        ],
    }).encode()
    req = request.Request(ENDPOINT, data=body, headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {key}",
        "Content-Type":  "application/json",
    })
    try:
        with request.urlopen(req, timeout=TIMEOUT) as r:
            payload = json.loads(r.read())
    except error.HTTPError as e:
        detail = ""
        try:
            detail = e.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")[:500]
        except Exception:
            pass
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {e.code} {e.reason}: {detail}") from None

    try:
        return payload["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    except (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError):
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"unexpected response shape: {json.dumps(payload)[:400]}") from None

def transient(msg):
    m = msg.lower()
    return any(t in m for t in
               ("http 429", "http 5", "timed out", "timeout", "temporarily",
                "connection", "urlopen error", "reset", "unreachable",
                "incompleteread", "incomplete read", "broken pipe", "eof"))

# ---------- job IO -----------------------------------------------------------

def write_result(job_id, obj):
    tmp = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, job_id + ".tmp")
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(obj, f, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())                      # survive power loss
    os.replace(tmp, os.path.join(OUT_DIR, job_id + ".json"))

def write_json_atomic(path, obj):
    tmp = path + ".rewriting"
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(obj, f, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())
    os.replace(tmp, path)

def discard(path):
    try:
        os.remove(path)
    except OSError as e:
        log(f"  could not remove {os.path.basename(path)}: {e}")

def quarantine(path, job_id, reason):
    log(f"[{job_id}] giving up -> failed/  ({reason})")
    try:
        stamp = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
        base  = os.path.basename(path)
        os.replace(path, os.path.join(FAIL_DIR, f"{stamp}-{base}"))
    except OSError:
        discard(path)

def process(path):
    job_id = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(path))[0]
    done   = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, job_id + ".json")

    if not os.path.isfile(path):                  # a directory named *.json, etc.
        return

    # Idempotency, but ONLY a success is final. A stale failure must not
    # poison the id forever -- resubmitting the same id has to work.
    if os.path.exists(done):
        try:
            with open(done, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                prev = json.load(f)
        except Exception:
            prev = None
        if isinstance(prev, dict) and prev.get("ok"):
            log(f"[{job_id}] already answered, dropping duplicate input")
            discard(path)
            return
        log(f"[{job_id}] previous attempt failed, retrying from scratch")
        try:
            os.remove(done)
        except OSError:
            pass

    # Read. A failure here may just be a mid-write producer, so we wait for
    # the file to go quiet before calling it malformed.
    parse_err = None
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            job = json.load(f)
    except (UnicodeDecodeError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
        parse_err = f"unparseable input: {e}"
    except OSError as e:
        parse_err = f"unreadable (locked?): {e}"

    if parse_err:
        first = FIRST_SEEN.setdefault(path, time.time())
        try:
            quiet = time.time() - os.path.getmtime(path)
        except OSError:
            quiet = 0
        if time.time() - first < STUCK_SECONDS or quiet < 5:
            return                                # still settling; try again
        log(f"[{job_id}] {parse_err}")
        write_result(job_id, {"id": job_id, "ok": False, "error": parse_err})
        quarantine(path, job_id, "stuck unreadable")
        FIRST_SEEN.pop(path, None)
        return
    FIRST_SEEN.pop(path, None)

    if not isinstance(job, dict) or not str(job.get("prompt", "")).strip():
        write_result(job_id, {"id": job_id, "ok": False,
                              "error": "missing or empty 'prompt'"})
        quarantine(path, job_id, "invalid shape")
        return

    attempts = int(job.get("_attempts", 0)) + 1
    log(f"[{job_id}] asking GLM (attempt {attempts}/{MAX_ATTEMPTS}) ...")

    try:
        answer = ask_glm(job.get("prompt", ""), job.get("system"))
    except Exception as e:
        msg      = str(e) or repr(e)
        in_grace = (time.time() - STARTED_AT) < GRACE_SECONDS and transient(msg)
        if in_grace:
            log(f"[{job_id}] startup grace, not counting attempt: {msg[:160]}")
            time.sleep(5)                         # network probably still coming up
            return
        if attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS and transient(msg):
            log(f"[{job_id}] transient, will retry: {msg[:200]}")
            job["_attempts"] = attempts
            try:
                write_json_atomic(path, job)      # never truncate the only copy
            except OSError:
                pass
            time.sleep(min(30, 2 ** attempts))
        else:
            write_result(job_id, {"id": job_id, "ok": False, "error": msg})
            quarantine(path, job_id, f"failed after {attempts}")
        return

    write_result(job_id, {"id": job_id, "ok": True, "answer": answer})
    log(f"[{job_id}] done ({len(answer)} chars)")
    discard(path)

# ---------- main -------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    for d in (IN_DIR, OUT_DIR, FAIL_DIR):
        os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)

    lock = acquire_lock()
    if lock is None:
        log("another watcher already running (port busy) - exiting")
        return

    log("=== GLM bridge v3 started ===")
    if not os.environ.get("LUMEN_API_KEY", "").strip():
        log("WARNING: LUMEN_API_KEY not visible to this process")

    for stale in (glob.glob(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "*.tmp")) +
                  glob.glob(os.path.join(IN_DIR, "*.rewriting"))):
        try:
            os.remove(stale)
        except OSError:
            pass

    backoff = 1
    while True:
        try:
            for path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(IN_DIR, "*.json"))):
                process(path)
            backoff = 1
        except Exception:
            log("loop error:\n" + traceback.format_exc())
            backoff = min(backoff * 2, 60)        # stop spamming the log
        time.sleep(backoff)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### `ask.py`

The producer side matters more than it looks. If you write the job file with a
plain `open(...).write(...)`, the watcher can read it halfway through. Write to
a name the watcher doesn't glob, then rename — rename is atomic on both NTFS
and POSIX filesystems.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Producer helper -- writes a job ATOMICALLY (tmp + rename) so the watcher can
never read a half-written file, then waits for the answer.

  echo "your prompt" | python3 ask.py [job_id]
"""
import os, sys, json, time, uuid

HERE    = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
IN_DIR  = os.path.join(HERE, "in")
OUT_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, "out")

def ask(prompt, system=None, job_id=None, timeout=300):
    job_id = job_id or uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]
    os.makedirs(IN_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    payload = {"prompt": prompt}
    if system:
        payload["system"] = system

    # .staging is not *.json, so the watcher cannot see it yet
    tmp = os.path.join(IN_DIR, job_id + ".json.staging")
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(payload, f, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())
    os.replace(tmp, os.path.join(IN_DIR, job_id + ".json"))   # atomic publish

    out      = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, job_id + ".json")
    deadline = time.time() + timeout
    while time.time() < deadline:
        if os.path.exists(out):
            try:
                with open(out, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    d = json.load(f)
            except Exception:
                time.sleep(0.5); continue
            if d.get("ok"):
                return d["answer"]
            raise RuntimeError(d.get("error", "unknown error"))
        time.sleep(1)
    raise TimeoutError(f"no answer for {job_id} within {timeout}s")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    jid  = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
    sysp = os.environ.get("GLM_SYSTEM") or None
    print(ask(sys.stdin.read(), system=sysp, job_id=jid))
```

### Autostart — macOS and Linux

Save as `install_autostart.sh`, then `chmod +x install_autostart.sh && ./install_autostart.sh`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# macOS -> launchd user agent;  Linux -> systemd user unit
set -euo pipefail

DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
PY="$(command -v python3)"
[ -z "$PY" ] && { echo "python3 not found"; exit 1; }

if [ ! -f "$DIR/.env" ]; then
  read -r -p "LUMEN_API_KEY=" KEY
  printf 'LUMEN_API_KEY=%s\n' "$KEY" > "$DIR/.env"
  chmod 600 "$DIR/.env"
fi

case "$(uname -s)" in
  Darwin)
    PLIST="$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/com.glmbridge.watcher.plist"
    mkdir -p "$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents"
    cat > "$PLIST" <<PLISTEOF
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN"
  "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.glmbridge.watcher</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>$PY</string>
    <string>$DIR/watcher.py</string>
  </array>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>$DIR</string>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>$DIR/launchd.out.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>$DIR/launchd.err.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
PLISTEOF
    launchctl unload "$PLIST" 2>/dev/null || true
    launchctl load  "$PLIST"
    echo "Installed launchd agent: $PLIST"
    ;;

  Linux)
    UNIT="$HOME/.config/systemd/user/glm-bridge.service"
    mkdir -p "$HOME/.config/systemd/user"
    cat > "$UNIT" <<UNITEOF
[Unit]
Description=GLM adversarial review bridge
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
WorkingDirectory=$DIR
ExecStart=$PY $DIR/watcher.py
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
UNITEOF
    systemctl --user daemon-reload
    systemctl --user enable --now glm-bridge.service
    loginctl enable-linger "$USER" 2>/dev/null || true   # survive logout
    echo "Installed systemd unit: $UNIT"
    ;;
esac
```

Two platform gotchas worth knowing, because both cost me time:

**launchd and systemd do not source your shell rc.** `export LUMEN_API_KEY=...`
in `.zshrc` is invisible to a service. This is the entire reason `watcher.py`
reads a `.env` file — it's the one mechanism that behaves the same on all three
platforms.

**`After=network-online.target` is a hint, not a guarantee.** Your service can
still start before DNS is genuinely usable. The 180-second startup grace window
in `watcher.py` exists for precisely this.

### Autostart — Windows

Save as `install_autostart.bat` and double-click it. `pythonw.exe` is Python
without a console window, so nothing sits in your taskbar.

```bat
@echo off
setlocal
set "PYW="
for /f "delims=" %%i in ('where pythonw 2^>nul') do if not defined PYW set "PYW=%%i"
if not defined PYW if exist "%USERPROFILE%\miniconda3\pythonw.exe" set "PYW=%USERPROFILE%\miniconda3\pythonw.exe"
if not defined PYW if exist "%USERPROFILE%\anaconda3\pythonw.exe" set "PYW=%USERPROFILE%\anaconda3\pythonw.exe"
if not defined PYW ( echo ERROR: pythonw.exe not found & pause & exit /b 1 )

set "LNK=%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\glm-bridge.lnk"
powershell -NoProfile -Command ^
 "$s=(New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell).CreateShortcut('%LNK%');" ^
 "$s.TargetPath='%PYW%';" ^
 "$s.Arguments='\"%~dp0watcher.py\"';" ^
 "$s.WorkingDirectory='%~dp0';" ^
 "$s.WindowStyle=7;" ^
 "$s.Save()"

start "" "%PYW%" "%~dp0watcher.py"
echo Installed. Starting now so you don't have to reboot.
pause
```

A Windows-specific trap: `setx` writes the registry but does **not** update any
already-open terminal. If you `setx` and then launch the watcher from that same
window, the process inherits an environment without your key. Either open a new
terminal, or — better — just use the `.env` file.

---

## Verifying it works

```bash
tail -f glm_bridge/watcher.log
```

You want to see:

```
[2026-09-16 14:56:15] === GLM bridge v3 started ===
```

and, critically, **no** `WARNING: LUMEN_API_KEY not visible` line under it.

Then a real round trip:

```bash
echo "Reply with exactly: BRIDGE OK" | python3 ask.py
```

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `WARNING: LUMEN_API_KEY not visible` | `.env` missing, or launched from a stale terminal |
| Log says `another watcher already running` | The single-instance guard working; an old copy is alive |
| Jobs pile up in `in/`, nothing in `out/` | Watcher not running, or crashed before the loop |
| Jobs landing in `failed/` | Read the `error` field in the matching `out/*.json` |
| Nothing in the log at all | Under `pythonw`/launchd, stdout goes nowhere — check the file, not a console |

---

## The part that actually taught me something

Everything above is the *finished* system. The first version was about sixty
lines and looked fine to me.

The moment the bridge worked, the obvious first thing to send through it was
the bridge itself. I asked GLM to review `watcher.py` as a hostile reader.

### Round one

It came back with twelve findings. Several were the kind of thing you nod at
and move on. Three were not:

> **Transient API failure = permanent job destruction.** On any exception from
> `ask_glm`, you write an `ok:false` result and `os.remove(path)` the input. No
> retry, no backoff, no distinction between "429 rate-limit," "120s timeout,"
> "DNS blip," and "malformed prompt." A 30-minute API outage annihilates every
> queued file, one per poll.

That one was correct and severe. My v1 deleted the job on *any* exception. A
rate limit would have quietly destroyed work.

> **No single-instance guard.** Boot task + manual launch = two pollers glob the
> same files, both call the API, both write results.

Also correct, and I had already created this exact situation: my installer both
registered the autostart entry *and* launched a copy immediately.

> **Log grows unbounded and spams on failure.** If the share disconnects
> mid-run, `glob` raises and you log a full traceback every second — ~40+ MB/day.

Correct.

But two of its findings were confidently wrong:

> **Environment at boot is wrong.** "At startup" tasks run as SYSTEM: user-scoped
> `LUMEN_API_KEY` isn't there...

This assumed Task Scheduler. I'd used a Startup-folder shortcut, which runs as
the logged-in user after login, with the user environment intact.

> **Login-time network/VPN race... `HERE` is presumably the mounted share.**

Also wrong: the watcher runs on native Windows against local NTFS. The mount
only exists on the *other* side of the bridge.

Both mistakes have the same shape. GLM was reasoning about a deployment it
couldn't see, and filled the gaps with the most common configuration. Which is
what a reviewer without context will always do.

### Round two

I fixed the real findings, then sent v2 back — this time explicitly supplying
the context it had lacked: Startup folder, runs as user, local NTFS, those two
concerns are moot.

The second review was much shorter, led with "structurally sound for this
deployment," and then found something better than anything in round one:

> Structurally sound. What's left is concentrated in one systemic flaw: **the
> idempotency check treats *failure* results as final, so any premature
> `ok:false` permanently poisons that job id.**

This was a bug I had *introduced while fixing the first batch*. To stop
duplicate API calls after a crash, I'd added "if `out/<id>.json` exists, skip."
Sound in isolation. But combined with the new failure-writing path, it meant a
single failed attempt permanently blacklisted that job id — resubmitting the
same job would be silently discarded as a duplicate.

It also caught that my claim about mid-write races was an assumption rather
than a fact:

> The comment "genuinely malformed, not a mid-write race" is an assumption, not
> a fact. The BOM tolerance hints the producer uses PowerShell — which is not
> atomic. Partial read → quarantined → the id is dead even after the producer
> finishes writing correctly.

It was right, and the root cause was on *my* side of the bridge: I'd been
writing job files with a plain redirect. That's what `ask.py` and its
tmp-plus-rename exist to fix.

### What I'd take from this

**Fixes introduce bugs, and the second review is where you find them.** The
worst bug in the whole exercise was one I created while patching the first
round. One pass of review would have shipped it.

**Supply the context, or you'll get confident nonsense.** Both of GLM's errors
were gaps filled with assumptions. Round two was dramatically better
specifically because I told it what it had gotten wrong.

**The reviewer's job is to generate candidates, not verdicts.** Roughly a third
of the findings were wrong or not applicable. Their value wasn't authority — it
was that I had to justify rejecting each one, which is a much better use of
attention than re-reading my own code hoping something jumps out.

**Different lab, different blind spots.** The point isn't that GLM is smarter.
It's that it was trained by different people on different data, so it fails
differently — and that's the entire value. A model reviewing its own output
shares its own blind spots by construction.

---

## What's still broken

Honest residual list, because a post that ends "and then it was perfect" is
lying:

- **One slow job stalls the queue.** Single-threaded; a job that times out can
  block everything behind it for minutes. Fixing it means concurrency, which
  for a personal one-job-at-a-time tool isn't worth the complexity.
- **The key sits in a plaintext file.** `chmod 600` is real protection against
  other users, and none at all against anything running as you. A keychain or
  credential-manager integration would be better.
- **The bridge only works while the watcher runs.** Close it and your agent
  silently loses the capability. The autostart entry is what makes this
  tolerable.
- **Polling, not events.** A one-second `glob` is wasteful and inelegant. It is
  also about fifteen lines shorter than anything using filesystem watch APIs,
  and works identically on all three platforms.
- **Not tested across a reboot at the time of writing.** The startup grace
  window is reasoned about, not yet observed.

---

## Generalizing

Nothing here is specific to GLM, or to Lumen, or to Claude. The pattern is:

> When an agent can reach your *files* but not your *network*, the filesystem
> becomes the transport.

That applies to an internal service behind a VPN, a database on your LAN, a
license-restricted API bound to your IP, a piece of hardware on a serial port.
The queue directory is the interface; what happens on the far side is nobody
else's business.

The specific thing I now get out of it: when Claude's confidence in an answer
is middling, it sends its own draft through the bridge, gets a critique from a
model trained by a different lab, and shows me both — along with which
criticisms it accepts and which it rejects, with reasons.

That last part is the bit I'd actually defend. Not the automation. The habit of
making a second, differently-wrong system argue with the first one, and then
having to adjudicate.

title: Giving Claude Write Access to Google Docs — When the Official Connector Can't
summary: From a read-only connector to a working Google Docs editing setup: Apps Script, a local MCP server, and the dead ends along the way.
